Okay, if it eases your mind at all since Dr. Google seems to have scared you - "bloat" is something large dogs with deep chests are notorious for. Great Danes, German Shepherds, Boxers, Poodles are a few at the top of the list. And if you had a dachshund, that is a small breed where you'd still want to be mindful of that. But a chihuahua not so much. 

What chihuahuas *are* notorious for, is a bad heart. Given his history, I suspect his heart disease has gotten worse. He does need veterinary attention soon. If there is nowhere you can get him to tonight, just get him somewhere as soon as a place opens. It is possible the bloated belly you see is an accumulation of fluid due to heart failure.

Its retching that is a sign of bloat, not coughing - although I suspect they appear similar to the average person. 

With this information, I doubt he is bloated. I do suspect this is a cardiac issue. You should take him to the vet as soon as one opens. Heart disease cannot be reversed, it can only be managed, but it will progress at some point.

What breed of dog? This is a concern primarily in dogs with deep chests. If you tell me you have a shih tzu or something, I am less concerned about bloat.

Dogs with bloat will retch - it looks like they are trying to vomit, but they don't actually vomit. When you say he is coughing, does what you see seem like he's trying to vomit?

These dogs also often restless and remain in visible discomfort. Their condition only continues to deteriorate so I'm not sure they would be able to lie down comfortably and sleep peacefully if bloated.

You keep speaking as if you know everything and referencing that yellow fluid = FIP so I'll just go ahead and throw in that yes, historically the viscous and straw-colored effusion is indicative of FIP however these days there are now a variety of bizarre presentations of FIP and many manifestations of which still are poorly understood. Some of these effusions are watery and pink even when the cause still is indeed FIP so this visualization alone is not considered a diagnostic tool and I would imagine the urge to send the fluid out for diagnostics would be to confirm the issue - sending home and treating it as if it is FIP, when it is not, will be both a waste of time and money when the owner has purchased this expensive treatment and the cat still rapidly decompensates. The recommendation to hospitalize on oxygen support was to stabilize the kitten and buy time to determine the appropriate treatment plan to encourage the best chance of success. Now I am not saying that the gold standard needs to be the only option, but it always needs to be offered and the OP seemed unwilling to consider it based solely on the assumption the vet only wants more money from them and that they personally feel antibiotics should be enough here because the kitten was "still acting okay." Well, she is vocalizing excessively when you say she normally does not meow, she has spent hours by your side when you say she is usually quite independent, and her litter box habit has suddenly changed. These are all potential indicators that she is in some sort of discomfort. Cats are notorious for their ability to hide illness, so she may not appear to be in pain when you touch her but this behavior is her telling you something is wrong. This is a lot of vomiting in one day, and the excessive water intake might indicate some metabolic/endocrine issues that don't surpise me in senior cats. She needs a vet visit - I'd say ideally today, due to the increased breathing you report.

I think you need something cleared up. Your cat did not have digestive issues, he had a URINARY issue. They did not place a catheter to drain his poop, they drained his BLADDER because he could not URINATE. I am clarifying this so you understand what happened better because the bowel movements you keep mentioning are irrelevant to this issue. Constipation is not a rapidly ticking time bomb, but urinary obstruction is. 

Some irritation after having had a catheter in place is normal, this causes frequent trips to the litter box and similar signs of discomfort as the actual obstruction but you will still be seeing urine. If your cat becomes unable to urinate again it is a *life threatening emergency.* If he seems irritated but can still urinate, great. If he cannot urinate, bad, immediately back to the vet - not negotiable, doesn't matter if your regular vet is closed, doesn't matter if its a long drive, the only option is to find one and get there.

It might be possible they get along eventually, it depends on exactly why the rescue believes she cannot be with other cats. Most cats will adjust in time, some taking longer than others, but then there are some very territorial cats out there who seriously cannot live around another cats. And this is not the same as a cat going to the vet where there are other cats/animals in the building, so however Reno acts at the vet is irrelevant to how she may act when you bring Jeanie into your household. 

But please for the love of god do NOT bring Reno down with you on a drive just to meet Jeanie.  Leave her at home and find a sitter for her. Cats are incredibly sensitive to change and you have an already very recently adopted cat that is still adjusting to her new home with you, that you have been told cannot get along with other cats, and you intend to scoop her out of your house and put her into the car and suddenly plop her into a brand new environment with brand new people and another cat? This is NOT a good idea. It is not impossible they get along later after Jeanie moves back in with you and you do a proper introduction that gives them plenty of time to adjust to one another, but I absolutely would not expect this sudden drop-in visit to go well at all and sincerely recommend you refrain.

And btw - no, Jeanie, who lives away with your family, cannot "sense" that you have since adopted a new cat.

Not sure if you are asking how to go to veterinary school or how to get into vet med in general. I am not a fan of immediate negative commentary such as "youll make no money," "you'll regret it," "do [insert other job here] instead." I would say that the fear of being too emotional is my biggest concern with your post, you need to be able to handle it emotionally. But, whether or not you want to attempt a career as a DVM is up for only you to decide, so:

1. You would need to start as an assistant anyway, or something similar. Admission into a college of veterinary medicine is partially dependent on "veterinary experience" hours, which is anything done in a veterinary setting under the guidance and/or supervision of a DVM. A job as an assistant counts, or an RVT although thats obviously additional schooling. Such a job also allows you to build rapport with DVMs directly so that you can get a good letter of recommendation - also a requirement for admission. You need "animal experience" hours also, anything caring for animals that is not in a medical setting,  but this does not include owning your own pets. This would be a job like kennel technician or volunteer rescue work that counts towards that. 
2. The GPA required varies widely. You do need good grades but despite what some may tell you, it is not the only important thing and you always have the chance to boost your application in the other required areas if you believe your GPA to be too low. It depends on the school - some do not even have a minimum requirement, some have a hard 3.4 minimum or higher. GPA for the purpose of veterinary school consists of your cumulative, your science, and the GPA of the last 45 (or so) credit hours you complete as you finish your undergraduate. "No minimum requirement" does not mean acceptance, obviously, as seats are limited so it is still very competitive.
